text: One sentence, spoken in a Council of Ministers in the summer of 1941, set the killing in motion on the Eastern Front. Radu Jude takes that sentence for his title and spends a hundred and thirty-eight minutes answering it rather than dramatizing what followed — a commentary, in Romanian, delivered with the patience of an argument that expects to be shouted down. Comedy sits among the listed genres, which looks wrong beside the subject until the method becomes clear: the target is not the past itself but the comfort of quoting it. It took the audience award at IFFR, an odd fate for a film built to be hard to sit with. What holds it is the distance between a phrase that can still be repeated lightly and the weeks that came after it was said.

Three middle-aged men stand in a river arguing about life while the rain comes down, and that is most of what happens. Jiří Menzel gives them seventy-four minutes: a swimming-bath owner named Antonin, a retired major, a canon, and then a traveling conjuror who lays a striped pole across the water, walks over it, and invites the town to a show. The comedy runs on how quickly settled men come unsettled by a stranger with a handstand and a beautiful assistant. Nobody in it is young. Everybody in it behaves as though a season could still change the terms of a life. Menzel keeps the scale domestic and the pace unhurried, and the argument, such as it is, arrives as weather: it rains, it clears, and the summer goes on being the sort of summer it is.

The knock comes in the middle of the night, and what walks in is family. Eszter and Farkas have a five-year-old and a working arrangement; Ernella and Albert have a daughter and a year in Scotland that did not take, which leaves them nowhere to go but a sister's flat. Szabolcs Hajdu holds it to eighty-one minutes and to rooms. Two households that were never in tune are sharing floor space now, with children present for all of it, and the pressure comes from the ordinary business of hosting: who sleeps where, who pays, how long is too long. The returning pair have no money and no version of the last year that flatters them. The hosts have the apartment, which turns out to be a kind of authority neither couple wants to name out loud.

Radiation is the antagonist that cannot be argued with, and the two physicists in this film keep working anyway. Mikhail Romm sets it inside the Soviet scientific community, where the danger produces no immediate sensation and offers no obvious moment to stop, and gives his men a long friendship and a shared attachment to a woman who declines to be arranged around either of them. A hundred and nine minutes, most of them talk: what a discovery is worth, what a career may cost the body conducting it, and the jokes men make when the alternative is saying something true. Soviet Screen named it the film of the year. The rivalry between the friends stays courteous throughout, which is by some distance the more uncomfortable arrangement.

The tour is a success, and that is exactly where the trouble starts. Petr Zelenka's film follows a documentary maker, Jan Holman, as he shoots a famous Czech singer-songwriter on the road with a folk band, and eighty-eight minutes later the toll has been taken out of the musicians and out of the man behind the camera in roughly equal measure. It is shaped like a documentary and filed as a comedy, and it declines to settle which it is; the songs, performed at length, are the part nobody could fake. What it understands about touring is that the machinery does not care whether the thing it carries is any good — success sets a schedule, and the schedule outlasts the enthusiasm of everyone obliged to keep it.

A man wants a drink of water; that is the entire offense, and it costs him the night. He comes in from the countryside, steps into a city apartment block, and is taken for a thief before he can get a sentence out. From there the building becomes a route — a hundred and thirty-seven minutes of stairwells, doors and balconies, each flat opening onto a household with something of its own to keep quiet — so that the man being hunted keeps stumbling into evidence against the people hunting him. Thriller and comedy at once, and neither one is softened: the chase stays frightening while the respectable residents conducting it grow steadily less respectable. Hindi, 1957, built on a single joke that is not funny for the man inside it.

The money was for a headstone, and a phone call takes all of it. Blaga is seventy, recently widowed, a former teacher with rules she has never had cause to test, and now she has an unmarked grave and a decision about what she will do to fix that. Stephan Komandarev gives her a hundred and fourteen minutes, and the precision of the film is that nothing in her collapses at once; the principles are amended one clause at a time, by a woman who would spot the amendment instantly in anyone else. Bulgaria sent it to the Academy that year. The fraud is the ordinary kind, run by voice down a telephone line, and the drama is not the theft but the arithmetic afterward: what a person of firm morals will let herself count as fair.

Krynica, in the 1960s: a working painter finds an old man installed in his studio and cannot get him to leave. Nikifor is deaf and mute, produces small pictures without pause, and is treated locally as a harmless eccentric; Włosiński has a career, a routine and no plan that includes a lodger. What Krzysztof Krauze follows over ninety-five minutes is less the discovery of a talent than the daily cost of housing one — the meals, the space, the rearrangement of one man's hours around another man's output. The friendship, when it comes, is practical well before it is warm. The paintings keep arriving, and the film treats them as work rather than as symptoms. Neither man is improved in the way films usually mean by that; both are altered, and only one of them had any say in it.

The rodeo circuit moves every week, which is most of its appeal to a man just out of prison. Frank T. Wells wants a few acres and the quiet that comes with them; Scarlett Stuart is running from a bank robbery that went wrong and cannot stay anywhere either. Genre supplies the rest — crime behind them, romance between them, a hundred minutes of American road — and Michael Karbelnikoff takes that arrangement at face value rather than winking at it. What the film has that the arrangement does not is the work itself: riding is a job with a schedule and a payout, the one thing a man with a record can do in public. Their version of the American Dream is small and portable and said out loud, which is either the honesty of the film or its ceiling.

Poland, 1948: a feature film set inside the Auschwitz extermination camp, in Polish, running a hundred and seven minutes. Wanda Jakubowska's central figure is Martha Weiss, a Jewish woman who arrives with her family and is assigned work as an interpreter — a position that keeps her useful to the people running the place and puts her between the women in the barracks and the orders concerning them. The register is procedural rather than lurid: arrival, assignment, work, the daily administration by which such a place was operated. What the film asks for is attention to routine, since routine is where its subject actually lived. It was made in the country where the camp stood, which shows in how little it stops to explain.

Everything here is measured at the height of an eight-year-old. The boy has a mother, a new man in the house and no vocabulary yet for what that man is supposed to be to him; Georgiy Daneliya, working from Vera Panova, keeps eighty minutes at that scale and declines to translate upward for the adults watching. The comedy is domestic and small, most of it produced by a child reading grown-up conduct literally, and the tact is in refusing to make the stepfather either a villain or a prize. What the boy is asked to do is accept a rearrangement he had no part in, inside a house that is still his. Filed as a family film, which is exact: the family is the problem, and the smallest person in it is the one expected to adjust.

The raft is the whole premise: three men who have not made time for one another in years finally take a long-planned trip down the Volga on logs. Alexander, Boris and Vasily have professions now, and that is the real subject — the way work becomes first a reason and then an excuse. Mikhail Kalatozov plays it for comedy, a hundred and two minutes of mishaps arranged along a river, each one a fresh occasion for accomplished men to behave like the younger versions of themselves who made the plan. The Volga does the structural work a plot would otherwise have to: downstream is a direction and also a deadline. Under the jokes sits an unembarrassed proposition about middle age — the friendship survives because somebody finally insisted on a date.

The flat keeps filling with animals, and the boy bringing them in has stopped explaining himself. Luis is fifteen; his method is to collect strays off the street, one after another, while his parents conduct a marital crisis at conversational volume and his grandmother's memory goes. Agustí Vila finds the comedy in the arithmetic — an apartment has a fixed number of rooms and the dogs and cats do not — and the drama in the fact that nobody in this family will say a plain sentence to anyone else. Miguel wants the collecting stopped. Alice indulges it. Neither position has much to do with the animals. Ninety-five minutes in which the silence of a household is measured by how much of it a boy has to fill with something living.

The Gulf War's sirens seal these people into one room together, which is how the film gets them introduced. Tel Aviv, and the immigrants in this building would otherwise have kept a polite distance: three stories run through the same arrangement, ninety minutes, each attack waited out in whatever company happens to be there. The sealed room is shelter and forced acquaintance at once. Arik Kaplun lets the situation do the comic work, since nobody here has the language or the money to be anywhere else. Karlovy Vary gave its best actress prize to the film's lead, which fits a picture that spends so long on a face listening for a noise to stop. What immigration costs gets counted in rent and proximity, not in speeches.
